blocks.text: AI 工具让智能体的 vibe 编程变得轻而易举。然而，在生产环境中构建和维护企业级智能体仍然要困难得多。尤其是，开发者往往被迫在质量（获得好的答案，尤其是在长尾任务上）和效率（在大规模下控制成本和延迟）之间做出取舍。通常，某些技术会以牺牲一个维度为代价来换取另一个维度的收益。

inlines.text: AI 工具让智能体的 vibe 编程变得轻而易举。然而，在生产环境中构建和维护企业级智能体仍然要困难得多。尤其是，开发者往往被迫在质量（获得好的答案，尤其是在长尾任务上）和效率（在大规模下控制成本和延迟）之间做出取舍。通常，某些技术会以牺牲一个维度为代价来换取另一个维度的收益。

blocks.text: 记忆是一种有望同时改善两者的方法。它可以帮助智能体跨任务携带有用的上下文，例如用户偏好、先前的纠正、指标定义和成功的工作流。原则上，这可以提高准确性、减少重复错误，并避免不必要的重复探索。但更多的历史记录并不一定意味着更好的记忆。提供每一次过去的交互成本高昂，并且可能引入过时、冲突或无关的上下文。核心挑战在于决定保留什么、如何维护它，以及如何衡量其有用性。

blocks.text: 在这篇文章中，我们介绍 MemCurrent，一种面向生产智能体的持久记忆架构，它现在为新的 Agent Bricks Memory 和 Genie 提供支持。智能体在工作时读写记忆，一个离线的“dreaming”流水线会整合记忆，使其保持一致和新鲜。在我们基于真实企业任务构建的内部基准上，MemCurrent 将智能体的通过率提升至无记忆时的三倍，同时使用的 token 减少了 31%，运行速度提高了 26%。本文的其余部分将介绍我们如何设计和评估它，以及我们在此过程中学到了什么。

blocks.text: MemCurrent 有两种记忆：情景记忆， 存储原始会话轨迹；以及派生记忆，包含从这些轨迹中提炼出的经验，以文件形式存储在结构化知识库中。顶部有一个自动生成的 memory.md 索引，描述文件结构以及每个文件的内容。

blocks.text: 情景记忆和派生记忆都存放在生产级数据库中，可扩展到大量用户，同时提供低延迟响应。情景记忆是仅追加的，插件会在会话运行时记录每一步。派生记忆是一张模拟分层文件系统的可变表，写入有两种方式。Agent 工具（add_memory, update_memory, delete_memory）处理显式请求，例如“永远不要在 /tmp 目录下写脚本”。离线 dreaming 流水线负责其余部分，将每个新会话中的隐式经验提炼到相关文件中。它还会清理整个存储，拆分过大的文件、合并重复项并解决冲突。

blocks.text: 读取是分层进行的。会话开始时，插件会注入记忆索引，让 agent 在开始前就知道自己掌握哪些知识。会话期间，agent 有两个可跨两种记忆类型使用的工具： search_memory 返回查询的最佳匹配项（过去轨迹中的某一步，或记忆文件中的某一行）， fetch_memory 按标识符（会话 ID 或文件路径）返回完整条目。

blocks.text: 此外，我们还基于真实的 Genie 对话构建了一个内部记忆基准测试，用户会在其中就自己的数据提出各种问题。如图 3 所示，我们从 12K+ 个会话出发，挖掘出 3K 个包含值得记忆信号的候选会话，并起草了一个带有评分标准的后续问题。同一用户的其余会话作为测试用例的填充内容。随后，一个对抗性评判器根据 7 项标准检查每个测试用例，例如知识是否确实存在、是否特定于该用户、是否为回答所必需、是否自然以及是否可验证。经过最终人工审核，该基准测试共有 114 个测试用例，涉及 29 个用户和 2,233 个历史会话。

blocks.text: 开源基准测试。 我们将每个记忆后端与一个简单的问答智能体配对，该智能体使用两种智能体框架（LangGraph 和 OpenAI Agents SDK）构建。我们还运行两个基线：下限为无记忆，上限为完整上下文，即每个过往会话都进入智能体的上下文。在所有三个基准测试中，MemCurrent 在所有记忆后端中得分最高，并且保持在成本-准确率帕累托前沿上。平均而言，MemCurrent（88.1%）的表现与完整上下文（87.8%）相当，而每个问题的输入 token 数约少 12 倍（8.4K 对 103K）。在历史最长的两个基准测试中，它甚至超过了完整上下文，因为把所有内容都塞进提示词反而会让智能体困惑。

blocks.text: 内部记忆基准测试。 在我们的基准测试中，差距进一步扩大。在这里，每个记忆后端都在我们内部的 Genie 中运行，该智能体与基准测试会话来自同一个智能体。历史记录太长，无法放入上下文，因此我们的上限是黄金注入：仅将黄金记忆注入智能体的上下文。在所有记忆后端中，MemCurrent 的通过率最高（68.4%），延迟最低（252s），token 使用量最低（418K），弥合了无记忆（22.3%）与黄金注入（78.6%）之间超过 80% 的差距。值得注意的是，虽然 Mem0 在较早的基准测试中也处于前沿，但在这里以 43.9% 落后，且延迟和成本更高。与无记忆相比，MemCurrent 使智能体的通过率提高到三倍（22.3% → 68.4%），同时速度提高 1.35 倍，成本降低 1.44 倍。

blocks.text: 为了理解 MemCurrent 卓越表现的原因，我们在 Internal Memory Benchmark 上针对两个设计选择进行了消融实验：记忆类型和提取策略。

inlines.text: 为了理解 MemCurrent 卓越表现的原因，我们在 Internal Memory Benchmark 上针对两个设计选择进行了消融实验：记忆类型和提取策略。

blocks.text: 我们需要两种记忆类型吗？ 仅情景记忆有中等帮助：35.8%，高于无记忆时的 22.3%。原始历史有用，但 agent 只在约三分之一的测试用例中搜索它，不过当它搜索时，其中 60% 能通过。派生记忆避免了这个问题，因为会话开始时注入的记忆索引让 agent 了解记忆中有什么以及何时查看，将通过率提升到 66.1%。在此基础上加入情景记忆可获得最佳结果，为 68.4%。增益很小，但它表明原始轨迹可以恢复蒸馏所丢弃的细节。

blocks.text: 什么是好的记忆提取策略？ 如图 2 所示，两个通道提取派生记忆：在线工具和离线 dreaming。单独使用时，离线 dreaming（63.5%）比在线工具（53.9%）高出近 10 个百分点。它们的组合产生了最高的通过率，为 66.1%。这支持了职责分工：dreaming 处理后台提取和整合，而在线工具让显式请求立即生效。

blocks.text: 结论

inlines.text: 结论

blocks.text: 记忆是智能体不再从零开始的方式。在本文中，我们介绍了 MemCurrent，这是一种面向生产环境智能体的记忆架构，它结合了情景记忆和派生记忆，并提供三种访问模式：自动记录和加载上下文的插件、智能体按需调用的工具，以及在后台整合记忆的离线 dreaming 流水线。

inlines.text: 记忆是智能体不再从零开始的方式。在本文中，我们介绍了 MemCurrent，这是一种面向生产环境智能体的记忆架构，它结合了情景记忆和派生记忆，并提供三种访问模式：自动记录和加载上下文的插件、智能体按需调用的工具，以及在后台整合记忆的离线 dreaming 流水线。

blocks.text: 在我们运行的所有基准测试中，MemCurrent 同时提升了质量和效率，这正是我们想要打破的权衡。在开源基准测试上，它以约 12 倍的输入 token 减少量达到了完整上下文的性能。在我们基于真实数据工作构建的内部记忆基准测试上，它将智能体的通过率提升至无记忆时的三倍，同时还使其更快、更便宜。

blocks.text: 消融实验指出了价值来源。派生记忆承担了大部分工作，而情景记忆通过恢复蒸馏过程中丢失的细节带来了较小的提升。将在线工具与离线 dreaming 相结合形成了最佳的提取策略：显式请求立即生效，而 dreaming 则在后台提炼隐式学习成果并整合存储。

blocks.text: AI tools have made it easy to vibe code agents. Building and maintaining an enterprise agent in production, however, remains significantly more challenging. In particular, developers are often forced to make a trade-off between quality (getting good answers, especially on long-tail tasks) and efficiency (keeping cost and latency in check at scale). Oftentimes, techniques bring gains in one dimension at the cost of another.

inlines.text: AI tools have made it easy to vibe code agents. Building and maintaining an enterprise agent in production, however, remains significantly more challenging. In particular, developers are often forced to make a trade-off between quality (getting good answers, especially on long-tail tasks) and efficiency (keeping cost and latency in check at scale). Oftentimes, techniques bring gains in one dimension at the cost of another.

blocks.text: Memory is a promising way to improve both at the same time. It can help agents carry useful context across tasks, such as user preferences, prior corrections, metric definitions, and successful workflows. In principle, this can improve accuracy, reduce repeated errors, and avoid unnecessary rediscovery. But more history is not necessarily better memory. Supplying every past interaction is costly and can introduce stale, conflicting, or irrelevant context. The central challenge is deciding what to retain, how to maintain it, and how to measure usefulness.

blocks.text: In this post, we introduce MemCurrent, a persistent memory architecture for production agents, which now powers the new Agent Bricks Memory and Genie. Agents read and write memory as they work, and an offline “dreaming” pipeline consolidates memory to keep it consistent and fresh. On our internal benchmark, built from realistic enterprise tasks, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate over having no memory, while using 31% fewer tokens and running 26% faster. The rest of this post covers how we designed and evaluated it, and what we learned along the way.

As a plugin (like our earlier work on MemAlign and Memory Scaling), memory is read and written automatically at fixed points in a session. As tools, the agent decides what and when to read and write. blocks.text: MemCurrent has two types of memory: episodic memory, which stores raw session traces; and derived memory, which has the distilled learnings from these traces, stored as files in a structured knowledge base. An auto-generated memory.md index sits at the top, describing the file structure and what each file contains.

inlines.text: MemCurrent has two types of memory:
episodic memory
which stores raw session traces; and
derived memory
, which has the distilled learnings from these traces, stored as files in a structured knowledge base. An auto-generated
memory.md
index sits at the top, describing the file structure and what each file contains.

blocks.text: Both episodic and derived memory live in a production-grade database that can scale to many users while delivering low-latency responses. Episodic memory is append-only, where a plugin logs each step as the session runs. Derived memory is a mutable table simulating a hierarchical file system, where writing happens in two ways. Agent tools (add_memory, update_memory, delete_memory) handle explicit requests like “Never write scripts in the /tmp dir”. An offline dreaming pipeline captures the rest, distilling implicit learnings from each new session into the relevant files. It also cleans up the whole store, splitting oversized files, merging duplicates, and resolving conflicts.

blocks.text: Reading works in layers. At session start, a plugin injects the memory index, so the agent knows what it knows before it begins. During the session, the agent has two tools that work across both memory types: search_memory returns the top matches for a query (a step in a past trace, or a line in a memory file), and fetch_memory returns the full entry by identifier (session ID or file path).

blocks.text: In addition, we built an Internal Memory Benchmark from real Genie conversations, where users ask all kinds of questions about their data. As in Figure 3, we started from 12K+ sessions, mined 3K candidates containing memory-worthy signals, and drafted a follow-up question with scoring rubrics. The other sessions from the same user serve as fillers for the test case. An adversarial judge then checked each test case against 7 criteria, such as whether the knowledge is actually present, specific to the user, required to answer, natural, and verifiable. After a final manual review, the benchmark has a total of 114 test cases, with 29 users and 2,233 history sessions.

blocks.text: We compare MemCurrent with three open-source memory backends, Mem0, PropMem, OpenClaw memory, using the same underlying LLM.

blocks.text: Open-Source Benchmarks. We pair each memory backend with a simple question-answering agent, built with two agent harnesses (LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK). We also run two baselines: a floor with no memory, and a ceiling with full context, where every past session goes into the agent's context. Across all three benchmarks, MemCurrent scores highest among all memory backends and stays on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. On average, MemCurrent (88.1%) performs on par with full context (87.8%) at ~12x fewer input tokens per question (8.4K vs 103K). On the two benchmarks with the longest histories, it even beats full context, where dumping everything into the prompt ends up confusing the agent.

blocks.text: Internal Memory Benchmark. On our benchmark, the gap widens. Here, each memory backend runs inside our internal Genie, the same agent the benchmark sessions came from. The histories are too long to fit in context, so our ceiling is gold injection: injecting only the gold memories into the agent's context. Among all memory backends, MemCurrent has the highest pass rate (68.4%) and the lowest latency (252s) and token usage (418K), closing over 80% of the gap between no memory (22.3%) and gold injection (78.6%). Notably, while Mem0 was also on frontier on earlier benchmarks, it trails at 43.9% here with higher latency and cost. Compared to no memory, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate (22.3% → 68.4%) while making it 1.35x faster and 1.44x cheaper.

blocks.text: MemCurrent in Action

inlines.text: MemCurrent in Action

blocks.text: In addition to benchmark numbers, let's examine two examples of how MemCurrent helps in practice, from internal Genie sessions.

inlines.text: In addition to benchmark numbers, let's examine two examples of how MemCurrent helps in practice, from internal Genie sessions.

blocks.text: Example 1: Memory stops an occasional hallucination mistake. In Figure 7, a user asked the agent for the top 20 users of Product X over the past two months. The agent wrote a correct SQL query, but never read the actual execution results saved to a file. It still confidently produced a table with hallucinated content. Upon user feedback, the agent saved the lesson to memory. Next time, once the query ran, the agent read the results first and returned the right table. One memory correction kept a one-off slip from becoming a habit.

blocks.text: Example 2: Memory saves computation on related tasks. In Figure 8, a user asked for “the top 5 SDP customers”. The agent had to figure everything out from scratch: what “SDP” stands for, which tables held usage data, and how to join and filter them. It took 11 tool calls, 8 subagents, and nearly six minutes. The agent saved these steps as a workflow file in memory, which it could reuse on related tasks. Later, the user asked a different question: how many SDP customers had more than 5K pipeline runs last month. Using the workflow, the agent answered with 2 tool calls and 1 subagent in 41 seconds. The question was new, but the path to the answer wasn't, and memory let the agent skip unnecessary exploration.

blocks.text: What Makes MemCurrent Work

inlines.text: What Makes MemCurrent Work

blocks.text: To understand what accounts for MemCurrent's superior performance, we ran ablations on our Internal Memory Benchmark for two design choices: memory types and extraction strategy.

inlines.text: To understand what accounts for MemCurrent's superior performance, we ran ablations on our Internal Memory Benchmark for two design choices: memory types and extraction strategy.

blocks.text: Do we need both memory types? Episodic memory alone helps moderately: 35.8%, up from 22.3% with no memory. The raw history is useful, but the agent only searches it in about a third of test cases, though it passes 60% of those when it does. Derived memory avoids this issue, as the injected memory index at session start gives the agent information about what's available in memory and when to look, lifting pass rate to 66.1%. Adding episodic memory on top gives the best result, at 68.4%. The gain is small, but it suggests raw traces can recover details that distillation drops.

blocks.text: What's a good memory extraction strategy? As shown in Figure 2, two channels extract derived memory: online tools and offline dreaming. When isolated, offline dreaming (63.5%) beats online tools (53.9%) by nearly 10 points. Their combination produces the highest pass rate at 66.1%. That supports a split of duties: dreaming handles background extraction and consolidation, while online tools make explicit requests take effect right away.

blocks.text: Conclusion

inlines.text: Conclusion

blocks.text: Memory is how an agent stops starting from zero. In this post, we introduced MemCurrent, a memory architecture for production agents that combines episodic memory and derived memory, with three access patterns: plugins to log and load context automatically, tools the agent calls on demand, and an offline dreaming pipeline that consolidates memory in the background.

inlines.text: Memory is how an agent stops starting from zero. In this post, we introduced MemCurrent, a memory architecture for production agents that combines episodic memory and derived memory, with three access patterns: plugins to log and load context automatically, tools the agent calls on demand, and an offline dreaming pipeline that consolidates memory in the background.

blocks.text: Across all benchmarks we ran, MemCurrent improves quality and efficiency at the same time, the trade-off we set out to break. On open-source benchmarks, it matches full context performance at about 12x fewer input tokens. On our Internal Memory Benchmark, built from real data work, it triples the agent's pass rate over no memory while also making it faster and cheaper.

inlines.text: Across all benchmarks we ran, MemCurrent improves quality and efficiency at the same time, the trade-off we set out to break. On open-source benchmarks, it matches full context performance at about 12x fewer input tokens. On our Internal Memory Benchmark, built from real data work, it triples the agent's pass rate over no memory while also making it faster and cheaper.

blocks.text: The ablations point to where the value comes from. Derived memory does most of the work, and episodic memory adds a smaller boost by recovering details that distillation drops. Combining online tools with offline dreaming makes the best extraction strategy: explicit requests take effect immediately, while dreaming distills implicit learnings and consolidates the store in the background.

blocks.text: Beyond the numbers, memory provides a knowledge base that isn't tied to a single agent or LLM. It can move with users to new agents or LLMs, and could seed knowledge shared across their organization, a direction we are exploring next.

inlines.text: For agent developers.
Agent Bricks is Databricks' developer platform for building custom agents. MemCurrent is built into Agent Bricks' Memory offering, powered by Lakebase. The offering includes:
Session store for episodic memory
Memory store for derived memory
An automatic dreaming pipeline
Tracing and evaluation of agent quality, including the impact of memory
A CLI which helps you quickly get started with an end-to-end sample agent with all of the above in <10 minutes
